questions.q: Across T-SQL, Oracle SQL, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake, what stays identical in the five-highest-priced-products example?
options: Only the table name stays the same
SELECT, the column list, FROM, and ORDER BY ... DESC
Nothing is identical -- every clause differs across all five
Only the ORDER BY clause stays the same; everything else differs
questions.explain: The core SELECT/FROM/ORDER BY structure is rock-solid standard SQL across all five platforms.

questions.q: Which three dialects in this lesson's example happen to agree on LIMIT n for limiting rows?
options: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake
SQL Server, Oracle, and MySQL
Oracle, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake
MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake
questions.explain: MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake all use LIMIT n; SQL Server uses TOP and Oracle uses FETCH FIRST ... ROWS ONLY.

questions.q: What syntax does Oracle use for limiting rows in this lesson's example, and what is notable about it?
options: Oracle has no way to limit rows at all
LIMIT n, identical to MySQL and PostgreSQL
TOP (n), borrowed directly from SQL Server
FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY -- the modern ANSI/ISO standard syntax, available in Oracle 12c and later
questions.explain: Oracle uses the newer standard FETCH FIRST ... ROWS ONLY syntax rather than TOP or LIMIT.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does basic SELECT syntax stay so consistent while pagination syntax doesn't?
options: Pagination is actually more standardized than basic SELECT syntax
Vendors deliberately break basic SELECT compatibility to force migration costs
Basic querying is the strongest part of the ANSI/ISO standard, while limiting rows is a feature each vendor historically implemented its own way before the standard addressed it
There is no real difference in pagination syntax across these platforms
questions.explain: This mirrors Lesson 1's three reasons for divergence -- row-limiting syntax predates, or was added separately from, standard adoption on each platform.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 1 end with a lesson emphasizing how SIMILAR the dialects are at the basic-query level?
options: To set a baseline, so the rest of the course can focus specifically on where the dialects genuinely diverge
To prove that this course has nothing further to teach after Chapter 1
Because the other dialects covered later in the course don't really exist in practice
Because basic querying is actually the hardest and most important topic in the course
questions.explain: Establishing where dialects agree sets up the rest of the course, which focuses on genuine divergence: data types, pagination detail, and procedural code.
